title: Montana's Big Sky Gets Even Bluer This Time of Year. Here's Why - Mix 97.1
content: I love fall in Montana. Summertime is my overall favorite, but fall in the Treasure State, despite how fleeting it can be, is pretty awesome. Backyard bonfires are better, sleeping is easier, the mosquitoes are gone, and we get to squirm back into all of our favorite cozy hoodies. Perhaps you've felt like the sky seems more blue this time of year. It's not your imagination. The Big Sky really does pop more in the fall and winter, and there are several reasons why. Read More: Hemorrhagic Disease Outbreak Hits Montana Deer And Antelope 1. No more forest fire smoke. This is an obvious (and much appreciated) factor for Montana's clearer, bluer skies in fall and winter. Typically from late May to September, much of our state is engulfed in smoke. 2. Fewer particulates in the air from other sources. Farm activity, pollen, and dust contribute to hazier skies in the summer months. 3. Dry air makes for bluer skies. In fall and winter, lower humidity and fewer tiny, suspended water droplets can leave the atmosphere looking cleaner, allowing that deep blue color to stand out. 4. The angle of the sun. Fall and winter sunsets can be dramatic, but the midday sky in Montana looks more blue this time of year as well, due to the lower angle of the sun. 5. Montana's elevation makes a difference. Much of Montana sits at a higher elevation than many other parts of the country. At higher elevations, there is less atmosphere above you, which can make the sky appear a deeper blue. 6. Surrounding seasonal colors can make the sky appear more blue.  A fresh layer of brilliant, white snow provides a ton of contrast with a blue sky. Another example would be the yellow, golds, and browns of fall trees and bushes against the backdrop of a blue fall sky. Dramatic color contrast can be quite pleasing to the eye.

title: TSM Shares Fall 1.8% Amid Chip Selloff Despite 69% Profit Growth - TOKENPOST
content: The decline coincided with a wider chip pullback as markets weighed an interest-rate hike and AI infrastructure costs. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) shares fell 1.8% on Oct. 15 as chip stocks sold off, despite strong quarterly results and guidance for another jump in fourth-quarter revenue. TSMC's U.S.-listed shares closed at $422.25 at 4 p.m. ET (20:00 UTC), down $7.75 from the previous close of $430. The decline coincided with a broader retreat in semiconductor stocks as markets weighed a possible interest-rate hike and the cost of building out AI infrastructure. The U.S. Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% through August. Prices also increased 0.6% from August on a seasonally adjusted basis. For the quarter ended Sept. 30, TSMC reported revenue of NT$1.49 trillion, up 50.9% in New Taiwan dollars. Revenue measured in U.S. dollars was $46.72 billion, an increase of 41.2%. Net income climbed 68.7% to NT$763.06 billion, and diluted EPS was $4.60 per ADR. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, which would be 58% higher year over year at the midpoint. Gross margin was 66.4% in the third quarter, down from 67.7% in the second. TSMC projected fourth-quarter gross margin of 65% to 67%, with a 66% midpoint. The company tied the expected dilution to the ramp-up of 2-nanometer production and overseas fabs. High-performance computing, which includes AI-related demand, made up 68% of third-quarter revenue. TSMC kept its 2026 capital budget at $60 billion to $64 billion and expects spending from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the prior three years. Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said demand for “our leading-edge technologies continues to be extremely robust.” TSMC also noted challenges for some consumer and price-sensitive markets from higher component prices and economic uncertainty, and said it was planning prudently for 2027. High NA EUV adoption planned for 2030, later than some competitors, potentially raising concerns about technology leadership timing. Power supply situation is a consideration factor in capacity planning, though currently assessed as manageable. AI demand calculation uses a narrow definition excluding CPUs, so the full extent of AI-related demand may not be fully captured in reported figures. Pricing strategy is strategic and varies by market segment, location, and technology, with US production costs higher than Taiwan, potentially affecting margins. Q: Laura Chen of Citi asked how TSMC views the AI revenue CAGR given aggressive AI semiconductor demand, and how it reconciles customer capacity requirements with concerns over data center power availability, funding, HBM, advanced packaging, and laser tightness.A: Chairman C.C. Wei explained that TSMC runs a sophisticated and disciplined capacity planning process, factoring in CSP CapEx, data center build-out, power supply, and other supply chain components. Based on its assessment, demand still exceeds supply, and TSMC is working hard to narrow the gap. CFO Wendell Huang added that demand is extremely robust with no sign of slowdown, and the AI accelerator CAGR will probably be higher than the previously guided mid- to high 50s percentage from 2024 to 2029. Q: Gokul Hariharan of JPMorgan asked whether wafer supply tightness in 2027 could be even greater than in 2026, and whether TSMC's wafer capacity growth could approach or exceed 10% in the next couple of years.A: C.C. Wei said demand is extremely robust and getting higher, with TSMC checking data center build-out and customer demand from multiple angles. The gap between demand and supply remains quite big, and TSMC is putting all its strength into increasing capacity. Wendell Huang added it is too early to discuss capacity increase percentages, but advanced nodes are the main driver of capacity growth. Q: Gokul Hariharan of JPMorgan also asked about TSMC's more aggressive overseas expansion, including potential new fab clusters in Texas and engagement with a customer's Terafab project.A: C.C. Wei confirmed TSMC is expanding in the US because most large customers are there and the US government is helpful. TSMC has evaluated locations outside Arizona, including Texas, and is in discussions with a customer about potentially utilizing Terafab capacity. He emphasized that any such fab must be run by TSMC, and more details will be shared once discussions conclude. Q: Krish Sankar of TD Cowen asked about a secondary wafer market where customers pass wafer allocation to others, and whether TSMC allows this practice.A: C.C. Wei stated this is not a new strategy and TSMC does not allow customers to sublet or auction off capacity. In certain cases, customers can collaborate through mask licensing agreements, but this is not common practice and the amount is very small. Q: Krish Sankar of TD Cowen also asked whether adopting High NA EUV later than competitors, around 2030, puts TSMC at a competitive disadvantage.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC always evaluates new tools for best technology, reasonable cost, and maturity. TSMC plans to use High NA in 2030 when it believes the tool will be mature and cost-effective, and is working with ASML on a 12-inch photomask by 2031. He emphasized TSMC remains confident it is still the best company to offer the most advanced technology to customers. Q: Charlie Chan of Morgan Stanley asked about an IDM customer spending aggressively on capacity and whether A14 could still be a bigger node than N2 despite potential insourcing.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC treats every customer fairly, whether IDM or fabless, and takes internal customer capacity into consideration. TSMC has seen more customer activity for A14 than for 2-nanometer so far and expects A14 to be a bigger node than N2. He declined to comment on specific customer outsourcing plans but guaranteed TSMC takes everything into consideration. Q: Charlie Chan of Morgan Stanley also asked about advanced packaging, including whether TSMC's SoW 3.5D can catch customers moving to larger reticle sizes like 14x, and whether TSMC would support customers if they cannot get sufficient capacity from a competitor's EMIB-T solution.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC's advanced packaging technology is very competitive, with the top priority being to help customers' products reach the market smoothly with best technology and enough capacity. TSMC is in real-world production of 5x reticle size with excellent yield, working on 9x and moving to 14x reticle size. CoWoS remains the number one choice for customers, and TSMC remains very competitive. Q: Sunny Lin of UBS asked how to think about CapEx beyond 2026, including whether CapEx could grow faster than or in line with sales, and whether tool price inflation is a meaningful variable for 2027 CapEx.A: Wendell Huang said it is too early to share CapEx numbers beyond this year, but TSMC has strong conviction in the AI megatrend, and CapEx from 2026 to 2028 is expected to be significantly higher than the past three years. Tool price inflation is real, but the majority of CapEx is related to long-term demand. He added that if TSMC does its job right, revenue growth will outpace CapEx growth. Q: Sunny Lin of UBS also asked about the wider 3% to 4% overseas margin dilution starting in 2027, and whether Arizona expansion is being accelerated.A: Wendell Huang said TSMC is doing everything it can to increase capacity and accelerating everywhere, including in the US. The 3 to 4 percentage point margin dilution from overseas fabs in the latter part of the five-year period remains the case. Q: Haas Liu of Bank of America asked about potential shifts in AI demand mix toward more efficient compute solutions, including agentic AI CPUs and networking switches, and the incremental opportunity for TSMC's manufacturing and packaging business.A: C.C. Wei said AI demand is extremely robust, whether from accelerators or CPUs, and TSMC has seen demand from agentic AI CPUs continue to increase. In TSMC's judgment, demand is still far above its ability to supply, and TSMC is working hard to narrow the gap. Q: Haas Liu of Bank of America also asked whether supporting both conventional power delivery and super power rail technology at future nodes makes the yield learning curve more challenging and impacts gross margins.A: C.C. Wei said the situation is different from previous years, with strong demand from both smartphone and AI HPC applications, and smaller die sizes and large accelerator die sizes happening at the same time. This is to TSMC's advantage because it has been prepared for this, results are excellent, and customers are very happy. title: Chip Leader TSMC Delivers Beat-And-Raise Third-Quarter Report - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: S&P 500, Nasdaq Break Support To Cap Ugly Week Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) on Thursday beat estimates for the third quarter and guided above views for the current period. But TSM stock fell after the report. The world's largest contract chipmaker, better known as TSMC, earned $4.60 per U.S. share on sales of $46.72 billion in the September quarter. Analysts polled by FactSet had expected TSMC to earn $4.46 a share on sales of $45.67 billion. On a year-over-year basis, TSMC earnings rose 61% while sales climbed 44%. In local currency, TSMC earnings increased 69% year over year in Q3 while sales rose 51%. For the current quarter, TSMC expects revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. The midpoint of $53.3 billion beat the consensus estimate of $50.22 billion. In the fourth quarter last year, Taiwan Semiconductor posted sales of $33.14 billion. One slight blemish on the quarter was TSMC's softening profit margins. TSMC's gross margin in the third quarter was 66.4%. It was 67.7% in the second quarter. For the fourth quarter, TSMC forecast a gross margin of 65% to 67%, or 66% at the midpoint. On the stock market today, TSM stock slid 1.8% to 422.25 amid the ongoing AI rout. TSM stock has tumbled since hitting an all-time high of 487.47 on Oct. 5. That occurred on the same day as its short-term breakout from a cup base with a buy point of 479, according to IBD MarketSurge charts. Chip stocks have been poor performers of late. The Philadelphia semiconductor index, known as SOX, fell for the seventh straight trading session on Thursday. It closed below its 50-day moving average line on Wednesday. The SOX, which includes the 30 largest chip stocks traded in the U.S., has fallen 12.4% since its Oct. 6 close. TSMC makes chips for a host of fabless chip designers including AMD (AMD), Apple (AAPL) and Nvidia (NVDA). Lately it has benefitted from high demand for chips for data centers running artificial intelligence applications. In the third quarter, shipments of 2-nanometer chips accounted for 8% of TSMC's total wafer revenue. Shipments of 3-nanometer chips accounted for 33% of revenue. Further, 5-nanometer chips accounted for 28% of wafer revenue and 7-nanometer accounted for 10%. Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and smaller node sizes, accounted for 79% of the company's total wafer revenue. "Our business in the third quarter was supported by strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies," Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said in a news release. "Moving into fourth quarter 2026, we expect our business to be supported by continued strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology." TSMC maintained its 2026 capital expenditures budget at $60 billion to $64 billion, with 2026-to-2028 capex expected to be significantly higher than the prior three years. The higher spending reflects the need to increase production capacity to meet continued strong demand for AI chips. TSMC is building 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan over the next several years and another five to six fabs overseas, Wedbush Securities analyst Matt Bryson said in a client note. He maintained his outperform rating on TSM stock and increased his price target on the company's Taiwan-traded shares. At least four equity analysts raised their price targets on TSM stock after the company's earnings report. "Management's tone was emphatically constructive: agentic AI is broadening silicon demand beyond accelerators into CPUs (central processing units) and networking, customers keep raising their requirements and demand still runs ahead of supply," Freedom Broker analyst Egor Tolmachev said in a client note. Tolmachev kept his buy rating on TSM stock and raised his price target to 560 from 475. Needham analyst Charles Shi reiterated his buy rating on TSM stock and raised his price target to 560 from 530. "TSMC reported strong results for Q3 with revenue above the high end of the guidance, and guided Q4 well ahead of the Street," Shi said in a client note. "We are increasing our 2027 and 2028 estimates. We expect 2027 is likely a banner year for TSMC in terms of reaching record revenue and sustaining high growth." Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSM) shares fell 2% despite strong quarterly results as a sector-wide sell-off weighed on the contract chipmaker. TSMC reported a sixth straight quarter of record profits, with the company's bottom line jumping nearly 69% while revenue surged 51%. The Taiwan-based contract chip manufacturer's sales are expected to reach as much as $54.3 billion for its current quarter, beating analyst estimates. "Demand for our leading-edge technologies continue to be extremely robust," TSMC CEO C.C. Wei said during the call. "We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance." Third quarter gross margin was 66.4%, down from 67.7% in the second quarter. TSMC expects a gross margin of 65% to 67% for the fourth quarter. "Given the continued robust multi-year demand from our customers, including the emerging agentic AI market, we reiterate our full-year 2026 capital budget to be between $60 billion and $64 billion," TSMC CFO Wendell Huang said. The company expects capital expenditures from 2026 to 2028 "to be even more significantly higher than the past three years," as it continues to invest heavily to support customers' growth, Huang added. The company is closely tied to the AI infrastructure build-out and its execution, as it manufactures advanced processors designed by chip giants such as Nvidia (NVDA), AMD (AMD), and Broadcom (AVGO). TSMC stock is up more than 41% year to date as of Wednesday's close. title: TSMC CEO Hints Company Could Step In If Intel Cannot Meet Customers’ Advanced Packaging Demand - Stocktwits
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) CEO C.C. Wei hinted during the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker could step in if customers struggle to secure enough advanced-packaging supply from Intel (INTC). The remarks came after Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan asked whether TSMC would support customers that initially chose Intel’s EMIB-T packaging technology but later faced supply constraints, according to the Koyfin transcript of the company’s third-quarter (Q3) earnings call. “I try to avoid answering it directly, but let me say that, yes, we will be,” Wei said. “Number one priority I already indicated is that TSMC’s customer’s product can be introduced into the market smoothly. That’s a number one priority. Okay? And that gives you enough of a hint.” TSM stock fell nearly 4% in morning trade amid broader market weakness as concerns around AI spending and hotter-than-expected producer prices weighed on markets. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment behind the chip supplier to companies like Nvidia (NVDA) and Apple (AAPL), improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Platform data showed a 666% increase in chatter in the same time period. Intel’s EMIB-T and TSMC’s Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) are competing approaches to advanced packaging that connect chip components and high-bandwidth memory into integrated systems used in AI computing. A shortage of packaging capacity can delay deliveries even when the underlying chips are available. Should that happen, clients can either delay their launch or switch to a different supplier. During Intel’s second-quarter (Q2) earnings call in July, CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated that  EMIB-T orders were growing and yield and reliability targets were being met, with the company preparing to scale production to support customers’ 2027 ramps. INTC stock fell over 5% in morning trade on Thursday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the company continued to trend in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day. Wei said TSMC is already producing packages five times the standard reticle size, with plans to expand to nine times and eventually 14 times that size. “We are in the real-world production of 5x reticle size. I don’t believe that anybody can do that today except at TSMC, and the yield is excellent,” he said. “So our customers are very satisfied with the result.” Wei added that the company is also working to reduce packaging costs, stating that its CoWoS technology remains customers’ preferred option. TSM stock fell in morning trade on Thursday despite reporting a Q3 earnings and revenue beat. Earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.91, according to Koyfin, beating Wall Street expectations of $0.89 per share. Revenue rose 50% year-over-year to $46.12 billion, beating analysts’ forecast of $45.69 billion. This was the company’s sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings. It forecast fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue would rise as much as 61% as compared to a year ago. TSM stock has gained over 36% this year. It’s currently trading around 14% below its record high of over $487 seen earlier this month. Apollo Global Management (APO) Chief Economist Torsten Slok stated that the Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy choice as producer prices accelerate and consumers begin pulling back on spending, raising the risk of an uncomfortable mix of persistent inflation and slowing economic growth. “This is a definition of stagflation,” Slok said during a CNBC interview. “We have higher prices, and in response to higher prices, we buy less.” His comments came after U.S. producer price inflation accelerated sharply in August, defying expectations for a decline. The annual producer price index (PPI) rose to 6.3%, its second-highest level in four years, higher than the expected 5.5%. Monthly headline PPI climbed 1.3%, more than double the 0.6% increase economists had expected. Core PPI also exceeded expectations, with the monthly reading coming in at 0.7% against an estimate of 0.3%. U.S. equities traded lower ahead of the PPI data release. After markets opened, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were on track to hit their worst week since June. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.4%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 1.3%. Meanwhile, SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) stayed in the green, with gains of around 0.44%. SPY and QQQ were among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. According to Slok, the hotter inflation reading complicates the Fed’s efforts to balance price stability against the risk of slowing growth. Slok said policymakers must decide whether to prioritize rising inflation or signs that consumers are beginning to rein in spending. “The challenge for the Fed is: Should they be focusing on inflation going up, or should they be focusing on the slowdown in consumers’ money and the risk of GDP growth?” he said. Slok pointed to housing and autos as early examples of interest-rate-sensitive sectors responding to tighter financial conditions. Mortgage rates have climbed substantially from their pandemic-era lows, while financing and leasing a car have become more expensive. “The more interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy are beginning to respond,” Slok said. “We’re seeing that in housing. We’re seeing that in autos.” He added that consumers are also showing early signs of adjusting their spending as higher prices squeeze household budgets. Slok also warned that the U.S. economy has become increasingly dependent on AI investment, leaving growth vulnerable if companies slow spending on data centers and related infrastructure. “GDP growth is normally two [percent], and now roughly one percentage point of GDP is coming from the AI spending boom,” he said. A slowdown in the build-out could weigh on economic growth even without triggering a recession. The key question, Slok said, is whether the financial returns from AI investment arrive as quickly as investors expect. “What if that payoff does not arrive with the speed that the consensus was expecting?” he said. Slok expects some moderation in data center construction as expectations for earnings and investment returns adjust, but does not anticipate a recession. “I think the answer is that we will not get a recession, but I do think we’ll get some more dampening of the data center build-out,” he said. With PPI inflation at its second-highest level in four years, CME FedWatch data put the odds of a Fed rate hike at 27.1% in October. Taiwan Semiconductor reported its Q3 2026 results with revenue and net income both sharply higher than a year earlier, extending its record-profit streak to a sixth straight quarter. The results beat estimates on demand tied to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Its current-quarter sales guidance also landed above what analysts had modeled. On the earnings call, Chief Executive Officer C.C. Wei stated that demand for Taiwan Semiconductor’s leading-edge technologies remains extremely robust, pointing to rising adoption of agentic AI. “The AI market continues to be very strong,” Wei declared, adding, “We did not see any sign of slowdown.” One soft spot sits in gross margin, which narrowed from the preceding quarter. Taiwan Semiconductor builds the advanced processors other companies design, so its results read as a demand signal for the whole chip complex. The company pioneered the pure-play foundry model and manufactures for fabless designers and integrated device manufacturers, with fabs across Asia, Europe, and North America. Advanced packaging extends Taiwan Semiconductor’s reach beyond wafers, and management described chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) packaging as customers’ top choice. A partnership on silicon interposers is also aimed at easing a significant backend shortage. Intel takes a different path, designing and fabricating its own chips across a manufacturing footprint in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. Its Intel Foundry business also offers process technologies and advanced packaging to outside customers. AMD represents the other end of the spectrum, leaving manufacturing to foundries while it designs server processors, graphics chips, and AI accelerators. Skeptics of Taiwan Semiconductor stock point to the fact that shares ran hard into the report and had already priced in a good quarter. Selling into a record result fits that pattern, and the narrower gross margin gives skeptics a fresh talking point. Management attributed the decline primarily to dilution from the initial ramp of its newest process node. Overseas fabs add further cost pressure, though productivity gains and capacity optimization across nodes provide a partial offset. Taiwan Semiconductor’s capital spending is also set to climb well above recent levels, and management said, “If we do our job right, the increase in revenue will outpace the increase in CAPEX.” Demand still exceeding supply anchors the bull case. Wei said, “Based on our assessed demand, we still think the demand is higher than the supply, and we are working very hard to narrow the gap.” That pull is broadening with the shift “from chatbot to AI assistants,” and capacity expansion in Taiwan, Arizona, and Japan gives the company room to capture more of it (we highlighted seven non-chipmaker suppliers riding the same buildout, from power to cooling, in a free AI infrastructure report). Taiwan Semiconductor’s next quarterly report could show whether its margin trajectory holds as capital spending rises. Management expects dilution from overseas fabs to widen in the next few years as more U.S. capacity comes online. For the iShares Semiconductor ETF, the open variable is the market’s appetite for AI hardware after record results from the sector’s bellwether foundry failed to steady chip stocks. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE:TSM) reported record third-quarter earnings on Thursday, exceeding market expectations as strong demand for advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence continued to support revenue growth. The world's largest contract chipmaker also confirmed that it was considering additional manufacturing facilities in the United States, including potential locations in Texas, as it seeks to expand production capacity. Net profit increased nearly 69% year-on-year to NT$763.06 billion ($23.55 billion) in the three months ended 30 September, exceeding the NT$746.3 billion consensus estimate based on Reuters/LSEG data. Revenue rose 50% to NT$1.49 trillion, reflecting continued demand for advanced chips from AI infrastructure providers and other technology customers. TSMC reported a gross margin of 66.4%, an operating margin of 58.7% and a net profit margin of 51.1%. The results marked the company's sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings and its eleventh consecutive quarter of growth. TSMC is evaluating further manufacturing investment in the United States as demand for advanced semiconductor production continues to increase. During the company's post-results webcast, Chief Executive C.C. Wei confirmed that TSMC had examined potential locations beyond its existing manufacturing operations in Arizona. "We're working very hard to increase our capacity in the U.S.," Wei said in response to an analyst's question. He added that Texas was among the locations being considered for additional facilities. Discussions remain ongoing regarding the structure of any new operations, including whether TSMC would develop and operate the facilities independently or collaborate with external partners. One potential arrangement mentioned involved Elon Musk's Terafab semiconductor manufacturing initiative. No final decision on the location, ownership structure or timetable for additional facilities was disclosed. The possible expansion forms part of TSMC's broader effort to increase production capacity as demand for advanced computing chips continues to exceed existing supply capabilities. Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang warned that TSMC's manufacturing expansion would continue to affect profitability margins as the company invests in additional capacity in Taiwan and overseas. Huang estimated that capacity expansion would dilute gross margins by approximately two percentage points in 2026. He also indicated that the impact from overseas manufacturing facilities could become more pronounced in subsequent years. For the fourth quarter, TSMC expects its gross margin to decline by at least 0.4 percentage points. The company anticipates substantially higher investment requirements in the coming years as it responds to continued demand from artificial intelligence customers. Huang said capital expenditure would be "significantly higher" in future periods, reflecting the need to increase semiconductor manufacturing capacity. TSMC maintained its 2026 capital expenditure budget of between $60 billion and $65 billion. However, Huang did not provide a specific forecast for how much additional production capacity the company expects to bring online over the coming months. The spending plans illustrate the financial commitments required to support demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, even as higher investment costs create pressure on near-term margins. TSMC expects revenue of between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion for the forthcoming reporting period, representing approximately 58% year-on-year growth, according to the company's guidance. Chief Executive C.C. Wei separately forecast that full-year 2026 revenue would increase by approximately 44% in US dollar terms. The projections reflect continued demand for advanced chips used in artificial intelligence computing, data centres and related applications. "The AI market continues to be very strong… we observe increasing AI demand, fueled by the increasing adoption of agentic AI," Wei said. He also highlighted the growing importance of semiconductor technology within the wider artificial intelligence industry. "The value of semiconductors in the global AI chain is expected to continue to increase," Wei added. The company's outlook suggests that investment in advanced AI systems remains an important driver of semiconductor demand despite broader concerns about technology sector valuations. TSMC's advanced manufacturing technologies continued to account for a significant proportion of its wafer revenue during the third quarter. The company reported that chips manufactured using its 2-nanometre process represented 8% of total wafer revenue. Its 3-nanometre technology accounted for a further 33%. These advanced production processes are used to manufacture high-performance semiconductors for applications requiring substantial computing power and improved energy efficiency. TSMC's manufacturing capabilities have positioned it as a major supplier to companies developing advanced AI processors. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) remains among its largest customers, reflecting the importance of TSMC's manufacturing capacity to the global AI computing industry. The company's results are closely monitored as an indicator of semiconductor demand across the wider technology sector. Its latest earnings followed strong results from semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML Holding (EU:ASML), which also reported continued demand associated with artificial intelligence earlier in the week. TSMC's results came during a period of considerable pressure on semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related equity valuations. Technology stocks have faced selling pressure as stronger US inflation figures increased expectations of further Federal Reserve interest rate rises. Higher borrowing costs have raised concerns about the financial implications of the substantial infrastructure investment required to support AI development. The market reaction has been particularly significant for companies relying heavily on debt to finance data centres, computing infrastructure and other expansion projects. Against that backdrop, TSMC's earnings demonstrated continued demand for advanced semiconductor production, although its own expansion programme is expected to weigh on margins. For investors, the company's ability to increase manufacturing capacity while managing capital expenditure and profitability will remain an important consideration as AI-related demand continues to grow. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) reported blockbuster third-quarter results, driven by robust demand for advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and high-performance computing (HPC). However, TSM stock fell sharply after the results. Revenue rose 16.2% sequentially and reached $46.72 billion, comfortably above analyst estimates of $45.41 billion. At the same time, earnings per share (EPS) came in at $ 4.60, beating expectations of $4.42 by about 4.1%. Despite the earnings beat, however, profitability showed signs of near-term trouble. Namely, gross margin declined 130 basis points from the previous quarter to 66.4%, while operating margin stood at 58.7%. As investors weighed the company’s aggressive expansion plans, rising capital expenditures, and mounting pressure on profit margins, TSM shares closed the session at $430, down 3.4% from the previous close. The price then fell another 2.1% to $420.98 in after-hours trading, leaving the shares approximately 5.5% below the previous closing price overall. The decline appears to suggest that investors are looking beyond earnings figures, focusing instead on the margins, future capital requirements, and the costs associated with international manufacturing expansion. While TSMC shares remain within the upper half of their reported 52-week range of roughly $266-$487, the market reaction indicates that strong AI demand might not be sufficient to ease concerns about the company’s growth strategy. Management itself attributed the pressure partly to the ramp-up of its next-generation 2-nanometer manufacturing technology and the continued expansion of overseas fabrication facilities. However, C.C. Wei, TSMC’s chairman and chief executive, still stressed the company’s expansion plans are going “full speed ahead:” “We are moving full speed ahead to increase our capacity to meet our assessed demand, and stepping up our CapEx investment to support our customers’ future growth,” Wei said. While confident, Wei’s tone probably did little to alleviate investor concerns, most of which were, as mentioned, focused primarily on unchecked expansion efforts. For now, then, management remains confident that demand will support further expansion, while the market worries whether TSMC can sustain its growth while managing the near-term costs. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3-$54.3 billion, implying approximately 14% sequential growth and 58% growth compared with the same period a year earlier. In addition, the company expects gross margin to range between 65% and 67%, while operating margin is projected at 56.5% to 58.5%. As for full-year 2026 results, management expects revenue to grow by approximately 44% and reaffirms its capital expenditure budget of 60-64 billion. However, TSMC expects capital spending between 2026 and 2028 to be significantly higher than during the preceding three years, which is another reason the shares took a hit. After all, the expansion includes a substantial increase in next-generation manufacturing capacity. More specifically, TSMC expects its 2-nanometer capacity to double in 2027. title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom - CNBC
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips. Here are TSMC’s third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate: The world’s largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier. TSMC’s third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company’s earnings call. The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand. TSMC’s stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company’s elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email. TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process. Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC’s careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems. “Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity,” he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers’ ability to deploy the chips they order. Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC’s total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips. By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate. TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors. The company’s free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago. TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain. TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule. TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona. The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence. Alcoa (AA) shares climbed overnight as CEO William Oplinger’s $315 million Massena East sale plan put asset sales in focus. The deal kicks off a push to unlock up to $1 billion by 2030, while tightening alumina supplies outside China could provide another tailwind. Alcoa stock traded over 1% higher overnight, ahead of Friday. However, the stock is down 4% so far this week. Alcoa is moving ahead with plans to unlock value from its assets, starting with a proposed sale of part of its Massena East site in New York that could bring in as much as $315 million. “We expect to receive the first $50 million to $65 million at closing, which is anticipated within 6 months, subject to customary permitting, regulatory approvals, key development and closing conditions,” said Oplinger during the third-quarter (Q3) earnings call. The remaining proceeds are expected before the end of 2030, although the agreement allows up to seven years for commissioning. Oplinger described the agreement as the first step toward Alcoa's goal of generating $500 million to $1 billion through asset sales and other monetization efforts by 2030. The arrangement could also provide additional payments as the data center develops and expands in the coming years. “It gives us some cash upfront, but it will give us cash further over the next 5 years as that data center first gets built and then gets increased in size. So it gives us a lot of upside.” Oplinger said alumina supplies became tighter outside China during the quarter, pushing prices to about $370 per metric ton. Alcoa expects supplies to tighten further in late 2026 and 2027 as production cuts, project delays and uncertainty over Indonesia’s new supply limit availability. AMC Entertainment Holdings Inc. (CEO) stock is headed for a second week of gains, and CEO Adam Aron has fired up his public feud with Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD) executives Vlad Tenev and Dan Gallagher, fiercely rejecting the retail broker's offshore stock tokenization plans, ahead of third-quarter (Q3) earnings. AMC Entertainment stock edged 0.3% lower overnight, ahead of Friday. The stock has gained 1.3% so far this week. On Thursday, Aron took to X to launch a blistering broadside against Robinhood, directly confronting its CEO Vlad Tenev and chief legal officer, Dan Gallagher, over the broker’s stock tokenization initiatives. Aron is concerned that Robinhood is creating digital tokens linked to AMC shares without the company’s permission. He called them “fake, synthetic shares” and warned that they could affect AMC’s ownership structure and control over its shares. “AMC Entertainment does not consent to Robinhood creating Stock Tokens to replicate AMC shares in the United States (the SEC requires you to get our consent, or failing that, at least with us to stand down). They are fake, synthetic shares, which could impact our capital structure.” “AMC should control our financial destiny, not Robinhood.” Robinhood’s stock tokenization program lets international investors trade digital tokens linked to U.S. stocks and ETFs around the clock. The tokens track stock prices but do not give holders direct ownership or voting rights. AMC argues that creating tokens linked to its shares without permission could affect its ownership structure and control. Last month, Johann Kerbrat, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Crypto and International at Robinhood, said the platform plans to add a feature that lets eligible stock token holders exchange their tokens for actual shares and gain voting rights. AMC CEO Adam Aron has opposed the initiative, stating that token holders could gain exposure to stock prices without receiving full shareholder rights. Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev has defended the program, saying companies should control shareholder rights but not every legal use of their shares. The confrontation comes ahead of AMC Entertainment’s expected Q3 earnings next month. According to Fiscal.ai data, analysts project $1.4 billion in revenue and a $0.16 per-share loss. Shares of Strive, Inc. (ASST) edged 0.4% lower overnight heading into Friday after the bitcoin treasury company priced a larger SATS preferred-stock offering at a discount, while CEO Matt Cole dismissed criticism of its five-year share-price history as “meaningless.” ASST stock ended Thursday’s regular trading session at $25.65, up nearly 4%. Strive priced 7 million SATS preferred shares at $90 each late Thursday, expanding the offering by 40% from the 5 million shares proposed on Tuesday. The offer price is 10% below the shares’ $100 face value. The offering therefore carries $700 million in total value and is expected to generate $630 million in gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and expenses. Settlement is scheduled for Oct.20. Cole said on X that he would discuss the details on The Hurdle Rate Podcast when the offering settles. Strive plans to use the proceeds for purposes including bitcoin purchases, income-generating investments, working capital, capital spending, complementary acquisitions and repurchases of ASST common stock or SATA preferred shares. Meanwhile, Cole pushed back against Fred Krueger, founder and investor at 2718.fund, who shared an image showing ASST down 92.9% over five years. Krueger’s fund borrows against bitcoin holdings to make monthly distributions to investors. “This five-year chart is meaningless,” Cole said. He pointed to Strive’s takeover of Asset Entities, which he called a failing company, and said: “Since then, Strive has outperformed Bitcoin.” The reverse merger, completed last year, combined Strive with Asset Entities, previously a digital marketing and content delivery company, to create a publicly traded bitcoin treasury business. Bitcoin was trading around $82,000 early Friday after recovering from a brief drop below $80,000 on Thursday. Earlier this week, Krueger warned that financing bitcoin purchases with preferred stock paying 13%-15% annual dividends could erode shareholders’ protection. Assuming bitcoin fell 33% over three years, his model deducted $891 million in bitcoin losses and $772 million in dividends from $3.56 billion in treasury assets. The remaining $1.90 billion matched preferred shareholders’ claims. “The entire common equity cushion is gone,” he said, leaving preferred holders with “essentially zero margin of safety.” The model assumed no new capital, operating income or other treasury changes and used the original $500 million offering, before its expansion to $700 million in face value. Cole dismissed the warning by pointing to Krueger’s support for BIP-110, a proposal to temporarily restrict non-payment data, such as images and text, in Bitcoin transactions. Cole suggested that the change could have triggered the downturn Krueger modeled. “Thankfully you were ignored then, and will be ignored now,” he said. SATS carries a $15 annual dividend per share, offering a 16.67% yield at the $90 offer price if paid in full. Payments are scheduled starting Nov.9, subject to board approval and available funds. Strive plans to reserve $157.5 million in existing cash and securities for the first 18 months of dividends. SATS holders rank behind SATA holders but ahead of common shareholders. Defending the company’s incentives, Cole said most rewards depend on “outperforming Bitcoin over a multi-year time period.” He cited a 64% increase in bitcoin per share this year. Separately, Strive disclosed buying 2,822 bitcoin for about $235 million during Oct. 12-Oct.13, bringing holdings to 35,595 bitcoin, according to Cole. Investors also exercised warrants covering 13.7 million common shares, generating expected gross proceeds of $369.2 million. title: Soros Capital Loads Up On MU, AMAT, AMD And TSM In Massive Semiconductor Pivot - Stocktwits
content: Soros Capital Management LLC more than doubled its equity portfolio to $559 million in the second quarter of 2026, pivoting away from industrials and energy toward semiconductors and AI-related technology. The semiconductor sector has been one of the market’s strongest performers this year, fueled by booming demand for artificial intelligence and shortages of memory chips that have pushed prices higher. Major tech companies are also pouring huge sums into AI systems, further boosting the sector. The firm’s most notable moves were large new positions in chipmakers and related suppliers, according to its filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday for holdings as of June 30. Micron Technology (MU) debuted with a $42.5-million stake, making it the second-largest holding. Applied Materials (AMAT) followed with a $34.5-million new position, while Flex (FLEX) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) entered with $32.2 million and $30.2 million stakes, respectively. ON Semiconductor was also newly added at $20.6 million. The firm’s biggest single addition was the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY) at $42.8 million, giving broad exposure to Korean chip giants. Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) saw its position surge more than 1,300% to $37.5 million. Caterpillar (CAT) nearly doubled to $34.9 million. These changes pushed technology and semiconductor exposure to dominate the top of the book. To fund the shift, Soros Capital, which manages assets for the Soros family, sharply reduced or exited several industrial and energy names that had been prominent in the prior quarter. Comfort Systems USA (FIX) saw the largest cut, down $22.4 million. GE Vernova (GEV) was trimmed by $11.3 million, while Bloom Energy, Analog Devices (ADI), and Emcor Group (EME) were also significantly reduced or sold. The portfolio now holds 58 positions, with the top 10 accounting for nearly 59% of assets. Micron, TSMC, Caterpillar, and Applied Materials sit among the largest stakes. Phillips 66 (PSX) and Marathon Petroleum (MPC) reportedly held merger talks earlier this year over a deal that would have created a $180 billion oil-and-gas giant. But the discussions ultimately fizzled out and are unlikely to be resurrected anytime soon, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Both PSX and MPC shares gained around 1% on Friday. At the time of writing on Friday midday, PSX stock was trading 0.15% higher, while MPC shares had pared all their gains and had edged down 0.05%. The talks taking place are a sign of the exuberance fueling mergers and acquisitions (M&A) under the Donald Trump administration, Semafor reported. A combination of Phillips 66 and Marathon Petroleum would have brought together businesses accounting for around a quarter of U.S. refining capacity and faced antitrust scrutiny, given there are only a handful of standalone refiners in the country. But administration officials have waved through a number of big mergers in other industries, including a $110-billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery and a $14-billion deal for Juniper Networks. Stanley Woodward, a top Justice Department official, has pushed to avoid trials in favor of settlements. A combined company would have been able to maintain a higher profit margin even when fuel prices dip, in part by negotiating stronger discounts from crude traders. The two companies also have a number of complementary businesses, including substantial pipeline and storage networks, although combining the operations would have been thorny. Phillips 66 has a joint venture with Chevron in chemicals, with each side having a right of first refusal to acquire the other side's wholly owned interest. Previous efforts by both Chevron and Phillips 66 to sell the business have reportedly run into hurdles. Marathon Petroleum also has a publicly traded but controlled subsidiary, MPLX, which would have added additional complexity to any combination. Future Fund managing partner Gary Black on Friday sharply shifted his view on a potential SpaceX (SPCX) acquisition of Tesla (TSLA), saying he now “fully expects” SpaceX to launch an all-equity offer at a healthy premium for Tesla sometime this year. “I fully expect $SPCX to make an all-equity offer at a healthy premium to acquire $TSLA sometime this year.  It makes Elon’s life easier, and there are clearly shared synergies,” Black wrote in a post on X. Just months earlier, Black dismissed the idea as highly unlikely. On May 22, he called a post-IPO merger “a very low probability event” with “no compelling business logic,” citing excessive dilution that would expand each firm’s market cap by 50% or more and a lack of clear synergies beyond Elon Musk’s control of both. In June and July posts, he reiterated that the “math won’t pass muster,” warned of fiduciary issues for SpaceX’s board, and labeled hopes of a buyout “greater fool theory.” His latest stance marks a clear reversal, driven by shared synergies and the deal’s potential to simplify Musk’s dual-CEO role. Black also predicts that many Tesla shareholders will sell on any announcement rather than wait 6-12 months for closing, citing intolerance of roughly 50% dilution and possible interim declines in the SpaceX shares received. Speculation about a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger has circulated for years, dating back well before SpaceX’s June 2026 IPO, as investors long noted the companies’ shared leadership under Elon Musk and overlapping ambitions in technology and manufacturing. The chatter intensified in early 2026 following SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI and reports that the rocket firm was weighing a combination with Tesla. After the IPO, the rumors surged further, centering on a possible all-stock deal to simplify Musk’s dual roles and capture synergies in AI, robotics, energy, and space. SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell addressed the speculation on the company’s June 12 IPO day. She told CNBC a combination “might make Elon’s life a little easier” and noted “no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX,” though she stressed her focus remains on operations. Tesla CEO Elon Musk, on the EV giant’s July 22 earnings call, pointed to “more and more overlap” from collaborations like the Terafab chip project but declined specifics, saying any combination must follow “the appropriate process.” On Friday, The Information also reported that Tesla is preparing to unveil a new design for its next-generation Roadster this month, which combines rocket technology from SpaceX for superior acceleration. Neither Tesla nor SpaceX, however, has confirmed merger talks. The Walt Disney Co. (DIS) CEO Josh D’Amaro on Friday acknowledged investor frustration with the company’s stock price, but said the company is in a strong position as it enters its next chapter, pointing to its streaming business, theme parks, ESPN and movie slate. During an interview with CNBC on the sidelines of the D23 Expo, D’Amaro said that he is “feeling pretty good” about where Disney is right now, nearly six months into his role as the company’s CEO. “I'm not happy with where the stock stands right now. Our investors aren't happy with that, but I do believe that we're sitting in a very great space relative to the entertainment industry,” he said. Disney shares were up more than 1% in Friday morning’s trade. D’Amaro said Disney’s intellectual property gives the company an advantage as entertainment companies increasingly seek to acquire valuable franchises, scale and complementary businesses. “If you look at what’s happening all around us, companies are trying to acquire scale or acquire IP or acquire additional businesses. And the reason that they’re trying to do that is because they want to look a little bit more like Disney,” he added. D’Amaro pointed to Disney’s extensive library of characters and franchises as a key asset that can drive value across its businesses. “We have the deepest library of intellectual property and characters and franchises by far,” D’Amaro said. “Our scale is enviable. The connection that we have with fans, you see it here, right here at D23, is palpable.” D’Amaro said bringing those assets together under a unified Disney strategy could be particularly powerful for the company. “We have everything that we need right now, putting those things together, under, I got to put one Disney frame, I think, is exceptionally powerful,” he added. D’Amaro said Disney’s next chapter will focus on continuing growth in streaming, improving margins, investing in its experiences business, moving ESPN toward direct-to-consumer and delivering strong films. He pointed to the company’s recent performance as evidence that its strategy is already producing results. “It is not just me hoping, it’s gonna happen. We’re actually delivering on that,” D’Amaro said, referring to Disney’s streaming growth, parks performance and other businesses. He also said the company wants to move with “more speed and urgency,” embrace technology more aggressively, and operate as “one Disney.” D’Amaro said Disney’s opportunity lies in getting consumers to engage with multiple parts of its business, from theme parks and Disney+ to merchandise and movies. “One of the things we know is that if a consumer is exposed to multiple parts of our business, there is a theme park visitor that then becomes a Disney+ subscriber, that Disney+ subscriber, then buys merchandise,” he said. D’Amaro said consumers who interact with multiple Disney businesses generate significantly more value than those who engage with just one part of the company. Disney wants to make those interactions more seamless and bring its businesses together under a unified consumer experience. “If it’s a seamless fan experience, I think that lifetime value goes up, and we drive top line and bottom line,” D’Amaro said. He also pointed to Disney+ as a potential centerpiece for that strategy, saying the company wants to bring more of its businesses and experiences onto the streaming platform. Shares of Valneva (VALN) stock surged 24% on Friday after the European Medicines Agency accepted the marketing application for its experimental Lyme disease vaccine for review. Valneva developed the vaccine in partnership with Pfizer (PFE). If it receives regulatory approval, Pfizer will have exclusive rights to manufacture and commercialize it. VALN stock recorded its biggest single-day gains since June 2022, and is currently trading at its highest levels since March. PFE shares edged 0.2% lower. The validation means the application can now undergo a formal scientific assessment, a crucial step ahead of launch across the European Union. However, it does not indicate that the vaccine, known as PF-07307405, will ultimately be approved. Lyme disease is a bacterial infection that can cause rashes, joint aches, fatigue and nerve issues. PF-07307405 is the most advanced Lyme disease vaccine candidate, and no human vaccine has been approved to date, according to Pfizer. “Lyme disease remains the most common vector-borne illness in Europe, affecting more than 100,000 people each year. When left untreated, it can lead to serious and potentially long-lasting complications involving the skin, joints, nervous system, and heart,” said Annaliesa Anderson, Senior Vice President and Chief Vaccines Officer at Pfizer. He was responding to Mach33 founder and CEO Aaron Burnett, who urged investors to study SpaceX while others were still catching up. Burnett’s post discussed Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas’ observation that few clients appeared to own the stock. In an excerpt shared by Tesla investor and influencer Sawyer Merritt, Jonas recalled asking 40 clients whether anyone owned SPCX shares. “Not a single hand went up,” he said. Jonas argued that assessing SpaceX solely through telecommunications, aerospace and defense, or AI misses the connections between its businesses. “Valuing SPCX is more of an ‘and’ problem than an ‘or’ problem,” he said. “The unusual dimensionality that makes it challenging to value the stock, in and of itself, gives the stock its value.” Burnett questioned why the “loudest” voices on asset pricing often had done the “least work” to understand underlying value, while acknowledging a place for both valuation shortcuts and technical research. “SpaceX is among the most difficult technology suites in the world to ‘intuit’ and getting more complex not less,” he said. “The complexity is equally a challenge and opportunity, depends on your perspective.” Wells Fargo said SpaceX is redeploying engineers from its launch and connectivity divisions to orbital data center work, prioritizing AI satellites ahead of a demonstration launch targeted for the second quarter of 2027. Vaxcyte said earlier on Monday that its experimental pneumonia vaccine, VAX-31, met the main goals of a late-stage study in adults 50 and older. The shot is designed to cover 31 strains of the bacteria that cause pneumococcal disease, which can lead to pneumonia, meningitis and bloodstream infections. In the study, immune responses were at least comparable to Pfizer’s Prevnar 20 and Merck’s Capvaxive on the strains those vaccines already cover, and stronger on three strains unique to VAX-31. Vaxcyte said the safety profile was consistent across the age groups tested. Vaxcyte shares rose 31% in regular trading and revived interest in vaccine makers. Novavax’s own story is about partnerships. In late August, the company said partners Sanofi and Takeda had won approval for an updated version of its protein-based COVID-19 vaccine, Nuvaxovid, in the United States, the European Union and Japan ahead of the 2026–2027 season. In the U.S., the shot is cleared for people 65 and older and for those 12 to 64 with a condition that raises the risk of severe illness. Sanofi holds the commercial rights in most markets and is carrying the vaccine into the fall season in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Canada. Novavax no longer sells it itself. It collects royalties on partner sales and is still due a $75 million manufacturing technology-transfer payment, which it has said it expects in the fourth quarter. Over the weekend, reports circulated that a Russian lab worker has died from a possible case of pneumonic plague while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. The reports are unconfirmed. According to a report from Axios, President Trump said on Monday that the U.S. will help Russia in case of a pneumonic plague outbreak. Axios also reported that the White House is monitoring the outbreak. Novavax, however, has no plague vaccine. A Stocktwits user noted that NVAX rallied during the Covid-19 pandemic, suggesting a similar rally could follow a plague outbreak. Another voiced optimism for more big pharmaceutical companies partnering with Novavax for its Matrix-M technology. Federal energy officials announced a conditional $4.2 billion loan commitment Monday to modernize and boost power production across nuclear generation facilities in Pennsylvania and Ohio, targeting rising regional electricity costs and surging energy demand. The funding, extended by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing to Texas-based utility operator Vistra (VST), aims to expand generation capacity across existing facilities without necessitating new power transmission infrastructure. According to department officials, the initiative supports executive measures to bolster domestic nuclear infrastructure and restore American energy output. The planned upgrades focus on Vistra’s Beaver Valley plant in Pennsylvania, along with the Davis-Besse and Perry facilities in Ohio. By executing thermodynamic and hardware uprates, the project will add 433 megawatts of power capacity while maintaining nearly 4 gigawatts of steady baseload electricity—enough to supply power to more than 3 million households. Earlier in January this year, Meta Platforms (META) struck 20-year agreements to buy power from Vistra’s Perry and Davis-Besse plants in Ohio and Beaver Valley plant in Pennsylvania. Beyond expanding immediate output, the modernization strategy will help extend operational life cycles at the three Midwestern plants by up to 20 years beyond their current licensing terms. The conditional loan arrangement also leaves open an option to fund future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak facility in Texas. Construction, engineering, and specialized maintenance during scheduled outage periods are projected to support about 3,000 temporary jobs while protecting thousands of permanent operational positions at the facilities. By boosting generation within established facility footprints, the funding addresses growing power consumption across the 13-state PJM Interconnection grid, which serves major industrial and residential centers throughout the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions. Final disbursement of the $4.2 billion loan remains contingent on Vistra meeting mandatory environmental, legal, technical, and financial criteria required by federal regulators. title: Nasdaq, S&P 500 Futures Slip As Iran Tensions, Chip Weakness Keep Investors On Edge: Why TSM, NVDA, NFLX, ATAI, ASTS Are In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock futures traded under mild pressure early Thursday as investors monitored escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and renewed weakness in semiconductor stocks against a backdrop of encouraging inflation signals and strong bank earnings in the previous session. Investors are also debating whether AI infrastructure spending has become overheated after the ‘Big Short’ investor Michael Burry mocked the data-center boom by calling it a "Fantasy," even as President Donald Trump described data centers as future "money machines" capable of generating jobs and tax revenue. U.S. military strikes on Iran continued for a fifth straight day, with Iran threatening retaliation. Back home, investors will be watching for initial jobless claims, among other economic data releases today. As of 4:00 a.m. ET, Nasdaq futures declined 0.5%, Russell 2000 futures were down 0.3%, S&P 500 futures fell 0.1%, and Dow futures were flat with a negative bias. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 Index, and the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, has remained ‘bullish’. SK Hynix Inc ADR (SKHY): The newly listed ADR remains volatile, tumbling over 11% in Seoul, leading a broader Asian semiconductor rout. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA): Trending on Stocktwits as it deepens its footprint in Japan, including partnerships with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Toyota and other enterprises. Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) is in focus after posting blowout June-quarter earnings, all thanks to booming AI demand. It has also formalized a $100 billion expansion plan to build four additional chip fabrication plants in the U.S. ASML Holding (ASML): Gaining momentum after smashing Q2 expectations and hiking its full-year 2026 revenue guidance. Retail traders have called it the “ultimate hardware gatekeeper.” AtaiBeckley Inc. (ATAI): Shares surged 43% in early premarket trade following reports that Eli Lilly (LLY) is negotiating a premium buyout valued north of $2 billion to expand its neuroscience portfolio. (ASTS): Shares fell 12% in early premarket trading after the company announced a $1 billion private offering of convertible senior notes, with management saying the proceeds could fund acquisitions and further vertical integration. Netflix (NFLX): Garners retail attention ahead of its earnings report, with investors watching subscriber trends, advertising momentum and management's outlook. Oil stocks (USO, BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX) remain in focus as crude supply chains brace for impact following Iran’s vow to exert control over the vital Strait of Hormuz. Other tickers trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing included Uber Technologies (UBER), Gorilla Technologies (GRRR), Transocean (RIG), Sandisk (SNDK) and Alibaba Group (BABA). On the economic front, investors will be tracking the release of the U.S. initial jobless claims, retail sales, the Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Index, and the pending home sales index. (TSLA) heads into next week's second-quarter (Q2) earnings with growing pressure from its retail investor base, as Robotaxi delays, missed milestones, and the Optimus production ramp dominate shareholder questions. TSLA stock is down 3% so far this week, with shares also down 0.3% in premarket trading on Thursday. Robotaxi is by far the dominant theme among the highest-ranked retail questions. The EV giant is expected to report its Q2 results on July 22. One of the most-upvoted submissions asks why Tesla has repeatedly missed its own autonomy targets: "Tesla has missed short term guidance on robotaxi 3 earnings reports in a row... What is keeping Tesla back from accomplishing these short term goals that they've set for themselves?" Another asks: "Why has growth of robotaxi vehicles stalled? When will we see Cybercab start customer rides?" Investors are also demanding concrete operating metrics, including fleet size, paid rides, intervention rates, cost per mile and revenue contribution, instead of broader progress updates. Others want revised rollout milestones after earlier targets were missed. Musk said in 2019 that Tesla could have one million Robotaxis on the road by the end of 2020, a target that never materialized as Full Self-Driving (FSD) remained a supervised system. Tesla reset expectations during its October 2024 Cybercab unveiling, targeting unsupervised Robotaxi operations in Texas and California in 2025 and volume production of Cybercabs in 2026. The company launched a limited paid Robotaxi service in Austin in June 2025 before beginning production of Cybercab earlier this year, though Musk cautioned that the initial production ramp would be "agonizingly slow." Optimus was the second most-discussed topic, with shareholders seeking updates on Gen 3 production, factory deployment and commercial rollout. The highest-ranked Optimus question asks about the Gen 3 production ramp, initial factory deployment and external sales timeline for 2027. Others ask how many Optimus robots are currently working inside Tesla factories, what tasks they perform and what manufacturing bottlenecks still stand in the way of mass production. The questions mirror Robotaxi concerns. Tesla first targeted limited Optimus production in 2023 before shifting toward low-rate production and internal factory deployment through 2026. Musk has said that the ramp for Optimus is also "agonizingly slow," arguing that nearly every component is new. Koyfin estimates call for Q2 revenue of $26.29 billion, up 17% from a year ago. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) is expected to rise 31% to $0.54. Morgan Stanley raised its price target to $417 from $415 and maintained an 'Equal Weight' rating, implying a 6% upside from current levels. The firm expects a solid quarter but continues to view Robotaxi and Optimus as the primary long-term value drivers. Barclays lifted its target to $370 and reiterated an 'Equal Weight' rating, implying a 6% downside, while Wells Fargo raised its target to $130 and maintained an 'Underweight' rating, implying a 67% downside. Jefferies raised its target to $400 from $375 while maintaining a 'Hold' rating, implying a 1% upside. The firm cited Tesla's delivery beat but warned that implied Cybercab production still points to further delays in the Robotaxi ramp. Blair thinks Stripe and Advent could go as high as $70 a share if pressed, though it puts a low probability on that happening. GameStop Corp. (GME) and Uber Technologies Inc. (UBER) have entered into a partnership to deliver everything from the latest game releases to consoles and accessories for on-demand or scheduled delivery across the U.S. The partnership marks another step in Uber Eats' push beyond restaurant deliveries as the platform continues adding retailers across categories such as groceries, electronics, beauty, and home improvement. For GameStop, the move offers another avenue to reach customers seeking faster access to gaming products without visiting a store. GameStop shares were up nearly 0.1% in Wednesday’s pre-market trade, while Uber shares were up about 1%. Customers can now order a wide range of products from participating GameStop stores through the Uber Eats app, including video games, gaming consoles, controllers, accessories, collectibles, and other consumer electronics. Orders can be placed for either on-demand or scheduled delivery, giving shoppers another way to purchase gaming products without visiting a physical store. Uber said the partnership is designed to make it easier for customers to get gaming essentials when they need them, whether it's replacing a controller before a game night, buying a newly released title on launch day, or picking up a last-minute gift. “Adding GameStop to Uber Eats strengthens our growing gaming and electronics selection, giving customers access to another trusted retailer they can shop with the speed and convenience they know from Uber,” said Uber’s Head of Grocery and Retail in North America, Hashim Amin. The addition also expands Uber Eats' growing selection of non-food retail offerings. To place an order, customers can browse the Retail or Electronics category in the Uber Eats app, search for GameStop, select their items, and choose a delivery time. Once the order is placed, customers can then track it in real time, similar to restaurant deliveries. GameStop is the latest retailer to join Uber Eats as the company continues expanding beyond restaurant deliveries. The platform recently added merchants across categories including beauty, office supplies, sporting goods, pet supplies, and consumer electronics as it seeks to become a broader marketplace for everyday shopping. Last month, Uber announced partnerships with retailers including Kiehl's, FedEx Office, Blick Art Materials, Academy Sports + Outdoors, and Choice Pet, adding thousands of additional storefronts to its marketplace. The company said the expansion builds on a retail network that already includes brands such as Sephora, The Home Depot, and Best Buy. Uber has said consumers are increasingly using the app for more than meals, prompting it to invest in new retail categories and on-demand delivery for a wider range of products. The addition of GameStop further expands its electronics and gaming offerings, giving customers another option for same-day delivery of consoles, games, and accessories. title: Taiwan Semiconductor’s Top Line Growth is Starting to Raise Eyebrows - 24/7 Wall St.
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor keeps raising its own growth targets while its share price moves in the opposite direction, and third-quarter results will determine whether that gap closes in investors' favor or widens into something more troubling. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM | TSM Price Prediction) trades at $445.16. September revenue rose 54.6% year over year, and in the same stretch the stock pulled back on AI spending fears. That leaves a gap between the business and the share price just before third-quarter results. Taiwan Semiconductor is the world’s largest dedicated foundry. It makes chips for Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) and Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) and sells no branded chips of its own. High-performance computing made up 66% of second-quarter revenue. The stock is up 47.62% year to date, but it fell 7.7% in the past week as chip stocks tumbled on AI spending fears and rising Chinese competition. Revenue for the first nine months of the year reached $122.12 billion, up 41.1%. Management now guides full-year growth to slightly above 40%, up from close to 30% at the start of the year. Second-quarter EPS came in at $4.31, ahead of the $3.89 consensus. Gross margin hit 67.7%, and net income rose 77.4%. The stock trades at about 21x forward earnings, compared with 33x trailing, and its PEG ratio is 0.858. Management expects strong demand “all the way to probably 2029, 2030”. A14 pilot production is set to begin in 2027. The 2nm ramp will cut gross margin by about 3 to 4 percentage points in the second half, and third-quarter margin guidance stands at 65% to 67%. Overseas fabs add more dilution, which management says could increase to 3% to 4% in later stages. The 2026 capital budget has been raised to $60 billion to $64 billion, and the company has committed another $100 billion to Arizona. September revenue slipped 0.6% from August. Management also admitted it is unsure whether demand will see “a dip” along the way. On top of that come customer concentration, Chinese competition and Taiwan geopolitical risk. The stock still trades above its 200-day moving average of $391.77. Consensus calls for third-quarter EPS of $4.46 on guided revenue of $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion. If gross margin lands near the 66% midpoint and fourth-quarter guidance holds firm, the case for upside gets stronger. A margin miss or a softer guide would point the other way. The average analyst target of $555.01 means 24.7% upside from $445.16. Targets are one data point and come with no guarantee. Of the 21 analysts covering the stock: Over the past year Taiwan Semiconductor gained 48.49%, while the S&P 500 rose 17.35%. Year to date the stock is up 47.62% against 14.1% for the index. The past week went the other way: the stock fell 7.7% while the S&P 500 slipped just 0.13%. Shares now sit below their 52-week high of $487.47. At $445.16, Taiwan Semiconductor trades below its 52-week high of $487.47. Revenue is accelerating, and the stock is moving the opposite way. September’s 54.6% growth ran well ahead of the 37% year-over-year midpoint in third-quarter guidance. That points to another quarter of upside on the top line. title: TSM Stock Spikes Overnight: Q1 Print Tops Estimates On Strong Demand For AI Chips, Advanced Processors - Stocktwits
content: U.S.-listed shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM) rose over 1% in overnight trading early Thursday after the chipmaker beat first-quarter (Q1) estimates on both revenue and profit as strong demand for 3nm chips and high-performance computing (HPC) continued to drive growth. TSM stock fell over 1% to $375.1 on Wednesday, but climbed marginally in extended trading. TSM reported net income of NT$572.48 billion ($18.14 billion) in Q1, up 58% from the previous year and above Fiscal AI estimates of NT$553.4 billion, while diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at NT$22.08, exceeding estimates of NT$20.96. The company also reported revenue of NT$1.134 trillion, rising 35% from a year ago and ahead of estimates of NT$1.117 trillion. Advanced process tech remained the backbone of TSM’s revenue growth during the quarter. 3-nanometer chips accounted for 25% of wafer revenue, while 5-nanometer chips contributed 36% and 7-nanometer chips represented 13%, with 7nm and more advanced technologies making up 74% of total wafer revenue. In U.S. dollar terms, quarterly revenue hit $35.9 billion, rising 41% from a year ago and 6.4% from the previous quarter. Meanwhile, gross margin for the quarter came in at 66%, operating margin reached 58%, and net profit margin stood at 51%. HPC continued to dominate the company’s revenue mix. The segment accounted for 61% of total revenue, underscoring its role as TSM’s largest growth engine, as AI-related workloads drive strong semiconductor demand. Smartphones contributed 26% of revenue, while IoT accounted for 6% and automotive for 4%. Revenue from high-performance computing increased 20% from the previous quarter, while smartphone revenue declined 11% from the prior quarter. Geographically, North America accounted for 76% of revenue, followed by Asia Pacific at 9%, China at 7%, and Japan and EMEA each contributing 4%.
